'''Philippe de La Hire''' (or '''Lahire''', '''La Hyre''' or '''Phillipe de La Hire''') (18 March 1640 – 21 April 1718)<ref name=Benezit>[http://www.oxfordartonline.com/subscriber/article/benezit/B00103126 "LA HIRE, Philippe de."] ''Benezit Dictionary of Artists''. Oxford Art Online (subscription required). Oxford University Press, accessed May 29, 2016.</ref> was a French [[painter]], [[mathematician]], [[astronomer]], and [[architect]].<ref name=Chareix662>Chareix 2008, p. 662.</ref> According to [[Bernard le Bovier de Fontenelle]], he was an "academy unto himself".

He was born in [[Paris]], the son of [[Laurent de La Hire]], a distinguished artist, and Marguerite Coquin.<ref>{{cite book |title=The Biographical Encyclopedia of Astronomers |last=Hockey |first=Thomas |year=2009 |publisher=[[Springer Publishing]] |isbn=978-0-387-31022-0 |accessdate=August 22, 2012 |url=http://www.springerreference.com/docs/html/chapterdbid/58635.html |archive-date=May 13, 2014 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140513011648/http://www.springerreference.com/docs/html/chapterdbid/58635.html |url-status=dead }}</ref> In 1660, he moved to [[Venice]] for four years to study painting.<ref name=Chareix662/>  Upon his return to Paris, he became a disciple of [[Girard Desargues]] from whom he learned [[geometrical perspective]]<ref name=Chareix662/> and was received as a master painter on 4 August 1670.<ref name=Benezit/> His paintings have sometimes been confused with those of his son, Jean Nicolas de La Hire, who was a doctor as well as a painter.<ref name=Benezit/>

He also began to study science and showed an aptitude for mathematics. He was taught by the French Jesuit theologian, mathematician, physicist and controversialist [[Honoré Fabri]] and became part of a circle formed by Fabri which included [[Giovanni Domenico Cassini]], [[Claude François Milliet Dechales]], [[Christiaan Huygens]] and his brother [[Constantijn Huygens, Jr.|Constantijn]], [[Gottfried Leibniz]], [[René Descartes]] and [[Marin Mersenne]].<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.faculty.fairfield.edu/jmac/sj/jg/jg4.htm |title=''Introduction to Jesuit Geometers'' by Joseph F. MacDonnell - Chapter 4 Influence on Other Geometers |access-date=2009-05-12 |archive-date=2021-11-30 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211130214338/http://www.faculty.fairfield.edu/jmac/sj/jg/jg4.htm |url-status=dead }}</ref> He became a member of [[French Academy of Sciences]] in 1678,  upon the death of [[Jacques Buot]], and subsequently became active as an astronomer, calculating tables of the movements of the Sun, Moon, and planets and designing contrivances for aiming [[aerial telescope]]s.<ref>[http://gallica.bnf.fr/ark:/12148/bpt6k3592w/f134.image.langEN "Méthode pour se servir des grands verres de lunette sans tuyau pendant la nuit"]. In: ''Mém. de l'Acad.'', 1715</ref> From 1679–1682 he made several observations and measurements of the French coastline,<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://bibnum.obspm.fr/exhibits/show/la-hire-english/la-hire-projets-english/la-hire-projets-carte-english|title=La Hire and the map of France · Philippe de la Hire, the Constant Study · Bibliothèque numérique - Observatoire de Paris|access-date=2021-05-03|archive-date=2021-05-03|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210503034420/https://bibnum.obspm.fr/exhibits/show/la-hire-english/la-hire-projets-english/la-hire-projets-carte-english|url-status=dead}}</ref> and in 1683 aided in mapping France by extending the [[Paris meridian]] to the north.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://bibnum.obspm.fr/exhibits/show/la-hire-english/la-hire-projets-english/la-hire-meridienne-english|title=La Hire and the Paris meridian · Philippe de la Hire, the Constant Study · Bibliothèque numérique - Observatoire de Paris|access-date=2021-05-03|archive-date=2021-05-03|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210503034422/https://bibnum.obspm.fr/exhibits/show/la-hire-english/la-hire-projets-english/la-hire-meridienne-english|url-status=dead}}</ref> In 1683 La Hire assumed the chair of mathematics at the [[Collège de France|Collège Royal]]. From 1687 onwards, he taught at the [[Académie royale d'architecture|Académie d’architecture]].

La Hire wrote on graphical methods, 1673; on [[conic sections]], 1685; a treatise on [[epicycloid]]s, 1694; one on [[Roulette (curve)|roulettes]], 1702; and, lastly, another on [[Conchoid (mathematics)|conchoid]]s, 1708. His works on conic sections and [[epicycloid]]s were based on the teaching of [[Desargues]], of whom he was the favourite pupil. He also translated the essay of [[Manuel Moschopulus]] on [[magic square]]s, and collected many of the theorems on them which were previously known; this was published in 1705. He also published a set of astronomical tables in 1702. La Hire's work also extended to descriptive zoology, the study of respiration, and physiological optics.

Two of his sons were also notable for their scientific achievements: [[Gabriel-Philippe de La Hire]], (1677–1719), mathematician, and {{ill|Jean-Nicolas de La Hire|fr|Jean-Nicolas de La Hire}} (1685–1727), botanist.

[[Mons La Hire]], a mountain on the Moon, is named for him.

On 19 December 1699, he presented ‘Expériences et observations sur les corps qui frottent l’un contre l’autre’ (Experiments and observations on bodies that slide against each other) at the [[French Academy of Sciences|Académie Royale des Sciences]] in Paris, where he proposed what are now commonly known as Amontons’ laws of [[friction]] after [[Guillaume Amontons]].<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Hutchings |first=Ian M |date=December 2021 |title=A note on Guillaume Amontons and the laws of friction |journal=Proceedings of the Institution of Mechanical Engineers, Part J: Journal of Engineering Tribology |language=en |volume=235 |issue=12 |pages=2530–2536 |doi=10.1177/13506501211039385 |s2cid=238729534 |issn=1350-6501|doi-access=free }}</ref>

== Selected works ==
[[File:Andromeda and Cassiopeia - Philippe La Hire, Planisphere celeste, 1705.jpg|thumb|right|250px|Andromeda and Cassiopeia, detail from ''Planisphère céleste'' (1705).]]
Unless otherwise stated, La Hire's works are in French.
* ''[http://gallica.bnf.fr/ark:/12148/bpt6k827559 Nouvelle méthode en géométrie pour les sections des superficies coniques et cylindriques]'' (1673) (New geometrical method for the sections of conical and cylindrical areas)
* [https://archive.org/details/bub_gb_kEscW3ubOS0C ''Nouveaux éléments des sections coniques: Les lieux géométriques: Les constructions ou effections des équations''] (1679)
* ''[http://echo.mpiwg-berlin.mpg.de/ECHOdocuView/ECHOzogiLib?mode=imagepath&url=/mpiwg/online/permanent/library/USVW0U1V/pageimg La gnomonique ou l'Art de faire des cadrans au soleil]'' (1682) ([[Gnomonics]] or the Art of making [[sundial]]s.)
* [https://books.google.com/books?id=oRgOAAAAQAAJ&pg=PR8 ''Sectiones conicæ''] (1685) ([[Conic section]]s.) {{in lang|la}}
* ''Tables du Soleil et de la Lune'' (1687) (Tables of the Sun and of the Moon)
* [https://books.google.com/books?id=AV01AAAAMAAJ&pg=PP7 ''L'ecole des arpenteurs''] (1689; on line: 4th ed., 1732)
* ''[https://archive.org/details/bub_gb_SCwPAAAAQAAJ Traité de mecanique: ou l'on explique tout ce qui est nécessaire dans la pratique des arts, & les propriétés des corps pesants lesquelles ont un plus grand usage dans la physique]'' (1695)
* {{Cite book|title=Tabulae astronomicae|volume=|publisher=Jean Boudot|location=Paris|year=1702|language=la|url=https://gutenberg.beic.it/webclient/DeliveryManager?pid=1455088}}
* ''Planisphère céleste'' (1705)
* [http://gallica.bnf.fr/ark:/12148/bpt6k34840/f198.image "Des conchoïdes en général"]. In: ''Histoire de l'Académie royale des sciences'', p.&nbsp;32 of the memoirs section (1708)
* [https://dx.doi.org/10.3931/e-rara-1564 ''Tabulæ astronomicæ Ludovici Magni iussu et munificentia exaratæ et in lucem editæ''] (1727) {{in lang|la}}
* [https://books.google.com/books?id=spwGTpg2DXoC&pg=PR1 ''Tables astronomiques dressées et mises en lumiere par les ordres et par la magnificence de Louis le Grand''] (1735)
